newsitem.title: USA: Governors propose alternative Medicaid plan.
newsitem.headline: Governors propose alternative Medicaid plan.

text.p: State governors Tuesday vowed to fight a White House plan to put annual spending caps on Medicaid, unveiling an alternative that cuts less and gives them more power over the nation's health programme for the poor.

The governors' new Medicaid budget plan breaks with President Clinton on another significant issue -- it does not include funding he wants to help expand health care to about half the 10 million U.S. children without health insurance.

Medicaid provides coverage for the poor, elderly and disabled serving about 37 million people. To help balance the budget, Clinton wants a per-capita limit on Medicaid spending. The programme is jointly funded by the states and Congress.
Governors say that by capping only federal spending, Clinton's plan shifts the risk to the states, forcing them to cut aid or raise taxes if caseloads were higher than expected.

"The (White House) proposal does drive change. The problem is all of the changes it drives are bad," Utah Republican Gov. Mike Leavitt told the Senate Finance Committee, testifying on behalf of the National Governors' Association.
Nevada Democratic Gov. Bob Miller said Congress had other options for balancing the budget aside from cutting Medicaid.
"I don't think anybody wants federal tax cuts at the expense of states having to raise taxes," Miller said.
But Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said he did not rule out caps on the programme.

The NGA plan calls for $8 billion in five-year Medicaid savings, compared to $22 billion in Clinton's plan. Governors, who have long chafed under federal rules, said they could get savings if Congress gave them more power to manage Medicaid.

They want to be able to set up managed care plans for the poor without special federal waivers, reduce the amount they must pay some health clinics and possibly require Medicaid recipients to pay a small monthly premium.
Governors also want to repeal a law they say forces high payments for institutional care. Clinton has proposed many of the same changes, but does not support copayments.

The NGA could not agree on the ticklish issue of aid to hospitals that serve a large number of the poor. Clinton wants to cut such payments by $15 billion. Many states have used such aid in the past to pad their own budgets.
Many of the cuts in Clinton's budget are ploughed back into the programme, for a net Medicaid reduction of $9 billion.
"We do not include savings for flexibility," said an administration official. "If governors are correct ... this would make it much easier for them to live within the cap."

Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm said the governors were dreaming if they thought they could get off with light cuts. "There's no possibility we will write a budget that doesn't have at least $26 billion in Medicaid savings," Gramm said.
Some Democrats suggested a standby cap that would go into effect if the governors did not achieve promised savings.
The governors did not seek more money for Clinton's plan to expand health coverage to children, although they said many states were already making aggressive efforts in that area.

Miller said Clinton's cap could discourage states from expanding benefits. The governors also warned it might not be possible to reach the White House goal of enrolling 3 million childen in Medicaid who are eligible but not receiving aid.

Republicans last session wanted $185 billion in six-year Medicaid savings. State reforms and other changes have reined in costs so that new estimates predict Medicaid spending will be $86 billion less than expected over the next five years.
